versions.text:
For more than two centuries, the stone well at the center of Tessendale had a habit shared by no other well in the county. On certain evenings it hummed, a low, steady note that rose from the shaft and carried as far as the churchyard. The villagers called it the Piper's Well, and few of them wanted it explained.

The name came from a story every child in the valley could recite. A young shepherd named Owen Marr, the tale went, played his pipe at the well-head each evening until a gust took his cap down the shaft. He leaned in after it, fell, and drowned, and ever since he had gone on playing below for anyone who stopped to listen.

In 1891 a county surveyor, Agathe Lorne, came to look into the matter. The miller, Josiah Fenn, assured her that the sound was his own wheel across the valley, carried through the rock, and the schoolmaster believed a stream ran beneath the well. Lorne kept a log for a season. The hum came on days when the mill was idle, and in dry weeks as readily as wet ones; what it always kept company with was a west wind. When she stretched a canvas sheet across the well's mouth one breezy evening, the piper fell silent at once. The sound, she wrote, was wind passing over the shaft, as breath passes over the neck of a bottle.

Her report caused more argument than the hum ever had. One councillor proposed filling the shaft with earth, and another wanted a stone slab laid over it. The women who drew water there every morning settled the matter by ignoring both, and by spring the proposals were forgotten.

On west-wind evenings the note still rises as the last buckets of the day come up, and anyone can hear exactly what Lorne heard: air moving over stone. It is a tidy answer. Yet the older people of Tessendale remember a sound that belonged to a drowned boy with a pipe, and it is hard to read Lorne's careful log without missing him a little.

For more than two centuries, the stone well at the center of Tessendale had a habit shared by no other well in the county. On certain evenings it hummed, a low, steady note that rose from the shaft and carried as far as the churchyard. The villagers called it the Piper's Well, and few of them wanted it explained.

The village council had other worries. After every heavy storm the well's water ran brown for days, and two families had fallen ill the previous autumn. In the spring of 1891 the council wrote to the county for a surveyor who could say whether the well was safe to keep.

The surveyor, Agathe Lorne, heard the theories first. The miller, Josiah Fenn, was sure the sound was his own wheel across the valley, carried through the rock, and a visiting naturalist had heard toads in the walls. Lorne kept a log through the summer. The hum came whether the wheel turned or stood, and long after the toads had gone quiet in June; it followed the rain, swelling in the weeks after a downpour. Lowering a weighted line, she found that the shaft opened at its base onto a hollow where an underground stream fell several feet. The falling water was the piper, and the same stream carried mud from the hillside into the well.

Some villagers asked for a pump to lift water from higher in the shaft, and the vicar wanted a stone slab laid over it so the hum could still be heard. The council judged the stream too close to mend. In October it drew twelve pounds from the parish fund for cartloads of earth, and once the ground had settled, turf was laid.

It is tempting to mourn the piper, but the legend has much to answer for. For decades it made the village treat a failing well as something sacred, and families went on drinking brown water out of respect for a drowned boy who, by every record Lorne could find, had never existed. Children now play ball on the square of grass by the church where he was said to play his pipe.

For more than two centuries, the stone well at the center of Tessendale had a habit shared by no other well in the county. On certain evenings it hummed, a low, steady note that rose from the shaft and carried as far as the churchyard. The villagers called it the Piper's Well, and few of them wanted it explained.

The earliest written report of the sound is an entry in the parish register for January 1702, in which the curate noted that the well "did sing all the night of the great frost, to the terror of the house next it." Later entries mention it in other hard winters, usually beside a remark about the cold.

In 1891 a county surveyor, Agathe Lorne, took up the question. The miller, Josiah Fenn, insisted the sound was his own wheel, carried through the rock, while the schoolmaster held that a stream ran under the well. Lorne kept her log from November to March. The hum came on frost nights whether the wheel turned or stood, and it was loudest when the ground was frozen hard and every spring on the hill had stopped. Descending on a rope, she found a long crack in the stone lining. As the stones shrank in the bitter cold, the edges of the crack rubbed and rang, and the shaft carried the note upward like a pipe.

The council's first thought was to fill the shaft with earth or cover it with a stone slab. Then Lorne's report appeared in the county newspaper, and it drew readers from as far as the coast who wanted to hear a well sing in the frost. The innkeeper, who had empty rooms every winter, argued for leaving it exactly as it was, and the council agreed.

Each January the inn is full again, and the lantern-lit path to the well, which has given no water since the spring house was built, is worn smooth. The legend, it turns out, had the details right. The old rhyme says the piper plays "when the ice is on the trough," which describes the conditions as exactly as Lorne's log, and it was set down by people with only their ears to go by.

For more than two centuries, the stone well at the center of Tessendale had a habit shared by no other well in the county. On certain evenings it hummed, a low, steady note that rose from the shaft and carried as far as the churchyard. The villagers called it the Piper's Well, and few of them wanted it explained.

The well was dug in 1640, when the village outgrew the spring on the hill. Its builders lined the shaft with dry stone, fitting the blocks without mortar, and left a ring of gaps just above the waterline where ground water could seep in. For two centuries it served the village well, apart from the hum.

In 1891 a county surveyor, Agathe Lorne, came to look into the matter. The miller, Josiah Fenn, was certain the sound was his own wheel, carried through the rock, and the schoolmaster blamed the west wind blowing across the well's mouth. Lorne kept a log from spring into autumn. The hum came on still nights as often as windy ones, and on Sundays, when the mill stood idle; it began in late May, ended by July, and came only after warm days. Lowering a lantern, she saw dozens of small brown toads crowded into the gaps in the lining. Their calls, echoed by the shaft, made the piper's note.

Once the cause was known, children crowded the low wall each June to peer at the toads, and the council feared a real drowning to match the legendary one. A pump was proposed and rejected as too costly, and one councillor wanted the shaft filled in. In the end the mason drew a heavy slab to close the shaft, and the village went back to the old spring on the hill.

So the drowned piper of Tessendale was a chorus of toads, and the shepherd who leaned too far over the wall was invented to explain creatures the size of a thumb. The old tale gave him a mournful tune; the toads, by Lorne's count, managed two notes. In early summer you can still hear them faintly through the stone, sounding rather pleased with themselves.

For more than two centuries, the stone well at the center of Tessendale had a habit shared by no other well in the county. On certain evenings it hummed, a low, steady note that rose from the shaft and carried as far as the churchyard. The villagers called it the Piper's Well, and few of them wanted it explained.

The person who finally explained it was Agathe Lorne, a county surveyor who had spent ten years mapping drains and quarries. She was known for distrusting any account she had not tested herself, and she arrived in Tessendale in the spring of 1891 with a notebook, a set of tuning forks, and a reputation for being rude to legends.

The villagers offered her explanations freely. The schoolmaster blamed the west wind blowing across the well's mouth, and a visiting naturalist had heard toads in the walls. Lorne kept a log for a season and compared it with the miller's account book. The hum came on calm days as well as windy ones, and in autumn as readily as in June; what matched it, day for day, was the record of grain going through Josiah Fenn's mill across the valley. The great wheel shook the rock beneath the valley as it turned, and the column of water in the well answered it like a struck glass.

The council considered filling the shaft with earth, since a well that trembled with the mill might one day crack, and the vicar proposed a stone slab to quiet it. Lorne's soundings showed the shaft solid and the water clean. As winter drew near, the council voted instead for an iron pump, so that nobody would have to lean over an icy wall to haul a bucket.

The well survived long enough to be explained only because of its legend. Three other wells in the parish were filled in during the 1880s, and the Piper's Well was spared because the village would not part with its drowned shepherd. The piper still plays on grinding days, though now he competes with the creak of a handle, and for that the village owes its old story a real debt.
